overview.text:
Recurrent neural networks process tokens sequentially, creating an inherent computational bottleneck that prevents parallelization across time steps. This sequential dependency severely constrains batch sizes and incurs massive computational costs when training on long sequences.

# The Sequential Bottleneck in Recurrent and Convolutional Sequence Models

Standard sequence transduction models have long relied on recurrent neural networks (RNNs), such as LSTMs and gated recurrent units, arranged in encoder-decoder structures. These models compute a sequence of hidden states $h_t$ one step at a time from the previous state $h_{t-1}$ and the current input token. Because each step depends on the one before it, you can't compute token representations in parallel during training. When sequences get long, memory limits constrain the batch sizes models can handle, driving up training times.

Convolutional approaches like ByteNet and ConvS2S were introduced to parallelize computation across all token positions. Even so, their operational path length between distant tokens scales unfavorably. In these networks, the number of operations needed to connect signals from two arbitrary positions grows linearly in ConvS2S and logarithmically in ByteNet. That scaling makes it tough for the network to learn relationships between distant words. While attention mechanisms had already been used to bridge distant positions, they were almost universally tethered to recurrent networks.

# The Transformer Architecture: Global Multi-Head Attention Without Recurrence

The Transformer replaces recurrence entirely with attention, connecting any two sequence positions in a constant number of operations. It keeps the familiar encoder-decoder framework: the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ into continuous representations $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, \dots, z_n)$, and the decoder generates output tokens $(y_1, \dots, y_m)$ auto-regressively, feeding its own previous outputs back in as inputs for the next step.

Both the encoder and decoder are built from stacks of $N = 6$ identical layers. Each encoder layer contains two sub-layers: a multi-head self-attention mechanism and a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. The decoder includes three sub-layers: a masked multi-head self-attention mechanism, an encoder-decoder multi-head attention mechanism that pulls information from the encoder stack, and a position-wise feed-forward network. Every sub-layer has a residual connection and layer normalization wrapped around it, producing outputs of the form $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$ with a uniform model dimension $d_{\text{model}} = 512$.

At its core, an attention function maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output vector, computed as a weighted sum of the values where each weight reflects query-key compatibility. The Transformer uses Scaled Dot-Product Attention, operating on matrices of queries $Q$, keys $K$, and values $V$:
$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$
Dot-product attention is faster and more space-efficient in practice than additive attention because it leverages highly optimized matrix multiplication routines. However, as the key dimension $d_k$ grows large, dot products grow in magnitude, which the authors suspect pushes the softmax function into regions with vanishingly small gradients. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ counteracts this growth. Inside the decoder's self-attention sub-layers, masking sets future position scores to $-\infty$ before the softmax step, ensuring predictions for position $i$ can't attend to ungenerated subsequent tokens.

{{figure:fig1}}

The flowchart above traces how Scaled Dot-Product Attention computes outputs: query and key matrices are multiplied, scaled down by $\sqrt{d_k}$, optionally masked to block future tokens, normalized into probabilities via softmax, and then multiplied by values.

Instead of running a single attention function across the full $d_{\text{model}}$ dimension, Multi-Head Attention projects queries, keys, and values $h$ times using learned parameter matrices. Scaled Dot-Product Attention runs in parallel on each projection:
$$\mathrm{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1, \dots, \mathrm{head}_h)W^O$$
where $\mathrm{head}_i = \mathrm{Attention}(QW^Q_i, KW^K_i, VW^V_i)$ with projection matrices $W^Q_i, W^K_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$, $W^V_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_v}$, and $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{\text{model}}}$. The base model sets $h = 8$ and $d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}} / h = 64$. This projection allows the network to attend jointly to information from different representation subspaces at different positions without increasing the computational burden relative to a single full-dimensional head.

{{figure:fig2}}

The comparison above contrasts a single attention function operating across the full model dimension against multi-head attention, which projects inputs into parallel lower-dimensional subspaces before concatenating and projecting them back to the base model dimension.

Each layer also includes a position-wise feed-forward network applied separately and identically to each position. It consists of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation between them:
$$\mathrm{FFN}(x) = \max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2$$
The inner dimension is $d_{ff} = 2048$, while input and output dimensions remain $d_{\text{model}} = 512$. Input and output embeddings share weights with the pre-softmax linear transformation, and embedding weights are scaled by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$.

# Positional Encodings and Structural Trade-Offs Across Sequence Layers

Because the Transformer doesn't use recurrence or convolutions, it doesn't have an innate sense of sequence order. To inject positional information, fixed sinusoidal positional encodings are added directly to the input embeddings at the base of both stacks:
$$PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right), \quad PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)$$
The authors hypothesized that sinusoids help the model attend by relative positions because $PE_{pos+k}$ can be expressed as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$ for any offset $k$, while potentially allowing the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths unseen during training.

Evaluating sequence layers across theoretical criteria reveals self-attention's structural benefits:
* **Self-Attention:** Operates with $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ complexity per layer, requires $O(1)$ sequential operations, and achieves an $O(1)$ maximum path length.
* **Recurrent Layers:** Incur $O(n \cdot d^2)$ complexity, require $O(n)$ sequential operations, and exhibit an $O(n)$ maximum path length.
* **Convolutional Layers:** Require $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$ complexity, $O(1)$ sequential operations, and an $O(\log_k(n))$ path length with dilated convolutions.

Self-attention's per-layer complexity is lower than recurrent layers whenever sequence length $n$ is smaller than representation dimension $d$, which is typical for subword machine translation representations.

For regularization, the base model applies residual dropout ($P_{drop} = 0.1$) to sub-layer outputs and embedding sums, along with label smoothing ($\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1$). Label smoothing forces the model to be more unsure, which harms perplexity but improves accuracy and BLEU. Optimization relies on the Adam optimizer with a learning rate that warms up linearly for $4000$ steps and decays with the inverse square root of the step number.

# Empirical Translation Benchmarks and Architectural Ablations

On the WMT 2014 English-to-German (EN-DE) benchmark, the base Transformer scored 27.3 BLEU using $3.3 \cdot 10^{18}$ FLOPs. The big Transformer achieved 28.4 BLEU with $2.3 \cdot 10^{19}$ FLOPs, surpassing the previous best ensemble (ConvS2S Ensemble at 26.36 BLEU and $7.7 \cdot 10^{19}$ FLOPs) by over 2.0 BLEU at lower training cost. On WMT 2014 English-to-French (EN-FR), the big model reached 41.8 BLEU in Table 2 (and 41.0 BLEU in the text) after 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs, establishing a single-model state of the art at less than a quarter of the training budget of prior leading models.

Ablations on EN-DE development data confirmed the importance of key architectural components:
* **Attention heads:** Single-head attention ($h=1$) degraded quality by 0.9 BLEU to 24.9, while too many heads ($h=32$) dropped BLEU to 25.4.
* **Key dimensions:** Reducing key size $d_k$ to 16 or 32 hurt performance (25.1 and 25.4 BLEU), suggesting that measuring query-key compatibility isn't trivial.
* **Positional encodings:** Learned positional embeddings achieved 25.7 BLEU, performing nearly identically to sinusoidal encodings (25.8 BLEU).

# Cross-Domain Generalization and Attention Head Specialization

To test generalization beyond translation, a 4-layer Transformer was applied to English constituency parsing. Trained solely on Section 23 of the Wall Street Journal Penn Treebank (roughly 40K sentences), it reached 91.3 F1 without task-specific tuning, outperforming several competitive baselines. In a semi-supervised setup with around 17 million sentences, it achieved 92.7 F1.

Visualizing encoder self-attention at layer 5 revealed that attention heads learned distinct, specialized behaviors. Certain heads captured long-range dependencies, such as connecting "making" to "more difficult" across intervening clauses. Other heads exhibited behavior interpreted as anaphora resolution, where attention originating from the pronoun "its" focused sharply on its antecedent.

# Core Insights, Architectural Trade-Offs, and Unresolved Frontiers

The Transformer shows that self-attention can replace recurrence and convolutions entirely, enabling parallelized training, cutting compute costs, and improving translation quality.

Still, important limitations remain. Autoregressive decoding is still sequential, generating one token at a time. Experiments were restricted to text, and scaling self-attention to long inputs like images, audio, or video requires local restricted attention mechanisms that weren't evaluated in this paper.

sources.text: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory [13] and gated recurrent [7] neural networks in particular, have been firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation [35]; [2]; [5]. Numerous efforts have since continued to push the boundaries of recurrent language models and encoder-decoder architectures [38]; [24]; [15].

Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states $h_t$ , as a function of the previous hidden state $h_{t-1}$ and the input for position $t$ . This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples. Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter. The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains.

The goal of reducing sequential computation also forms the foundation of the Extended Neural GPU [16], ByteNet [18] and ConvS2S [9], all of which use convolutional neural networks as basic building block, computing hidden representations in parallel for all input and output positions. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes it more difficult to learn dependencies between distant positions [12]. In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2.

Attention mechanisms have become an integral part of compelling sequence modeling and transduction models in various tasks, allowing modeling of dependencies without regard to their distance in the input or output sequences [2]; [19]. In all but a few cases [27], however, such attention mechanisms are used in conjunction with a recurrent network.

In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output. The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.

To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence-aligned RNNs or convolution. In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention and discuss its advantages over models such as [17]; [18] and [9].

Most competitive neural sequence transduction models have an encoder-decoder structure [5]; [2]; [35]. Here, the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations $(x_1, ..., x_n)$ to a sequence of continuous representations $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_n)$ . Given $\mathbf{z}$ , the decoder then generates an output sequence $(y_1,...,y_m)$ of symbols one element at a time. At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next.

The encoder is composed of a stack of $N=6$ identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. We employ a residual connection [11] around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization [1]. That is, the output of each sub-layer is $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$ , where $\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)$ is the function implemented by the sub-layer itself. To facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension $d_{\text{model}}=512$ .

The decoder is also composed of a stack of $N=6$ identical layers. In addition to the two sub-layers in each encoder layer, the decoder inserts a third sub-layer, which performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack. Similar to the encoder, we employ residual connections around each of the sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. We also modify the self-attention sub-layer in the decoder stack to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions. This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position $i$ can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than $i$ .

An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors. The output is computed as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight assigned to each value is computed by a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key.

In practice, we compute the attention function on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix $Q$ . The keys and values are also packed together into matrices $K$ and $V$ . We compute the matrix of outputs as:

The two most commonly used attention functions are additive attention [2], and dot-product (multiplicative) attention. Dot-product attention is identical to our algorithm, except for the scaling factor of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ . Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code.

While for small values of $d_k$ the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of $d_k$ [3]. We suspect that for large values of $d_k$ , the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients 1. To counteract this effect, we scale the dot products by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ .

sources.text: Similarly, self-attention layers in the decoder allow each position in the decoder to attend to all positions in the decoder up to and including that position. We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property. We implement this inside of scaled dot-product attention by masking out (setting to $-\infty$ ) all values in the input of the softmax which correspond to illegal connections. See Figure 2.

Instead of performing a single attention function with $d_{\text{model}}$ -dimensional keys, values and queries, we found it beneficial to linearly project the queries, keys and values $h$ times with different, learned linear projections to $d_k$ , $d_k$ and $d_v$ dimensions, respectively. On each of these projected versions of queries, keys and values we then perform the attention function in parallel, yielding $d_v$ -dimensional output values. These are concatenated and once again projected, resulting in the final values, as depicted in Figure 2.

$\begin{align*} \mathrm{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) &= \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head_1}, ..., \mathrm{head_h})W^O\\ % \mathrm{where} \mathrm{head_i} &= \mathrm{Attention}(QW_Q_i^{\dmodel \times d_q}, KW_K_i^{\dmodel \times d_k}, VW^V_i^{\dmodel \times d_v})\\ \text{where}~\mathrm{head_i} &= \mathrm{Attention}(QW^Q_i, KW^K_i, VW^V_i)\\ \end{align*}$

Where the projections are parameter matrices $W^Q_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$ , $W^K_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$ , $W^V_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_v}$ and $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{\text{model}}}$ .

In this work we employ $h=8$ parallel attention layers, or heads. For each of these we use $d_k=d_v=d_{\text{model}}/h=64$ . Due to the reduced dimension of each head, the total computational cost is similar to that of single-head attention with full dimensionality.

In addition to attention sub-layers, each of the layers in our encoder and decoder contains a fully connected feed-forward network, which is applied to each position separately and identically. This consists of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between.
$\begin{equation} \mathrm{FFN}(x)=\max(0, xW_1 + b_1) W_2 + b_2 \end{equation}$

While the linear transformations are the same across different positions, they use different parameters from layer to layer. Another way of describing this is as two convolutions with kernel size 1. The dimensionality of input and output is $d_{\text{model}}=512$ , and the inner-layer has dimensionality $d_{ff}=2048$ .

Similarly to other sequence transduction models, we use learned embeddings to convert the input tokens and output tokens to vectors of dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ . We also use the usual learned linear transformation and softmax function to convert the decoder output to predicted next-token probabilities. In our model, we share the same weight matrix between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation, similar to [30]. In the embedding layers, we multiply those weights by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$ .

Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence. To this end, we add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks. The positional encodings have the same dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ as the embeddings, so that the two can be summed. There are many choices of positional encodings, learned and fixed [9].
$\begin{align*} PE_{(pos,2i)} = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}) \\ PE_{(pos,2i+1)} = cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}) \end{align*}$

where $pos$ is the position and $i$ is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from $2\pi$ to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$ . We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset $k$ , $PE_{pos+k}$ can be represented as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$ .

We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E)). We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.

A single convolutional layer with kernel width $k < n$ does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Doing so requires a stack of $O(n/k)$ convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels, or $O(log_k(n))$ in the case of dilated convolutions [18], increasing the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network. Convolutional layers are generally more expensive than recurrent layers, by a factor of $k$ . Separable convolutions [6], however, decrease the complexity considerably, to $O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$ . Even with $k=n$ , however, the complexity of a separable convolution is equal to the combination of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed-forward layer, the approach we take in our model.

As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires $O(n)$ sequential operations. In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length $n$ is smaller than the representation dimensionality $d$ , which is most often the case with sentence representations used by state-of-the-art models in machine translations, such as word-piece [38] and byte-pair [31] representations. To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size $r$ in the input sequence centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to $O(n/r)$ . We plan to investigate this approach further in future work.

We apply dropout [33] to the output of each sub-layer, before it is added to the sub-layer input and normalized. In addition, we apply dropout to the sums of the embeddings and the positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder stacks. For the base model, we use a rate of $P_{drop}=0.1$ .
During training, we employed label smoothing of value $\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$ [36]. This hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score.
We used the Adam optimizer [20] with $\beta_1=0.9$ , $\beta_2=0.98$ and $\epsilon=10^{-9}$ . We varied the learning rate over the course of training, according to the formula:

overview.cited_text:
Recurrent neural networks process tokens sequentially, creating an inherent computational bottleneck that prevents parallelization across time steps. This sequential dependency severely constrains batch sizes and incurs massive computational costs when training on long sequences.

# The Sequential Bottleneck in Recurrent and Convolutional Sequence Models

Standard sequence transduction models have long relied on recurrent neural networks (RNNs), such as LSTMs and gated recurrent units, arranged in encoder-decoder structures [p00002, p00006]. These models compute a sequence of hidden states $h_t$ one step at a time from the previous state $h_{t-1}$ and the current input token [p00007]. Because each step depends on the one before it, you can't compute token representations in parallel during training [p00007]. When sequences get long, memory limits constrain the batch sizes models can handle, driving up training times [p00007].

Convolutional approaches like ByteNet and ConvS2S were introduced to parallelize computation across all token positions [p00010]. Even so, their operational path length between distant tokens scales unfavorably [p00010]. In these networks, the number of operations needed to connect signals from two arbitrary positions grows linearly in ConvS2S and logarithmically in ByteNet [p00010]. That scaling makes it tough for the network to learn relationships between distant words [p00010]. While attention mechanisms had already been used to bridge distant positions, they were almost universally tethered to recurrent networks [p00008].

# The Transformer Architecture: Global Multi-Head Attention Without Recurrence

The Transformer replaces recurrence entirely with attention, connecting any two sequence positions in a constant number of operations [p00009, p00010, p00013]. It keeps the familiar encoder-decoder framework: the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ into continuous representations $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, \dots, z_n)$, and the decoder generates output tokens $(y_1, \dots, y_m)$ auto-regressively, feeding its own previous outputs back in as inputs for the next step [p00015].

Both the encoder and decoder are built from stacks of $N = 6$ identical layers [p00017, p00018]. Each encoder layer contains two sub-layers: a multi-head self-attention mechanism and a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network [p00017]. The decoder includes three sub-layers: a masked multi-head self-attention mechanism, an encoder-decoder multi-head attention mechanism that pulls information from the encoder stack, and a position-wise feed-forward network [p00018]. Every sub-layer has a residual connection and layer normalization wrapped around it, producing outputs of the form $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$ with a uniform model dimension $d_{\text{model}} = 512$ [p00017, p00018].

At its core, an attention function maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output vector, computed as a weighted sum of the values where each weight reflects query-key compatibility [p00019]. The Transformer uses Scaled Dot-Product Attention, operating on matrices of queries $Q$, keys $K$, and values $V$ [p00021]:
$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$
Dot-product attention is faster and more space-efficient in practice than additive attention because it leverages highly optimized matrix multiplication routines [p00023]. However, as the key dimension $d_k$ grows large, dot products grow in magnitude, which the authors suspect pushes the softmax function into regions with vanishingly small gradients [p00024]. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ counteracts this growth [p00024]. Inside the decoder's self-attention sub-layers, masking sets future position scores to $-\infty$ before the softmax step, ensuring predictions for position $i$ can't attend to ungenerated subsequent tokens [p00018, p00034].

{Insert figure|fig1|Draw a flowchart showing Query and Key matrices entering a Matrix Multiply block, passing through Scale by 1/sqrt(d_k), an optional Mask block, a Softmax block, and multiplying with Values to yield the output.}

The flowchart above traces how Scaled Dot-Product Attention computes outputs: query and key matrices are multiplied, scaled down by $\sqrt{d_k}$, optionally masked to block future tokens, normalized into probabilities via softmax, and then multiplied by values [p00021, p00034].

Instead of running a single attention function across the full $d_{\text{model}}$ dimension, Multi-Head Attention projects queries, keys, and values $h$ times using learned parameter matrices [p00026]. Scaled Dot-Product Attention runs in parallel on each projection [p00026]:
$$\mathrm{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1, \dots, \mathrm{head}_h)W^O$$
where $\mathrm{head}_i = \mathrm{Attention}(QW^Q_i, KW^K_i, VW^V_i)$ with projection matrices $W^Q_i, W^K_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$, $W^V_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_v}$, and $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{\text{model}}}$ [p00028, p00029]. The base model sets $h = 8$ and $d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}} / h = 64$ [p00030]. This projection allows the network to attend jointly to information from different representation subspaces at different positions without increasing the computational burden relative to a single full-dimensional head [p00026, p00030].

{Insert figure|fig2|Draw a two-panel comparison showing single-head full-dimensional attention on the left versus parallel linear projections into h heads, scaled dot-product attention per head, concatenation, and final projection on the right.}

The comparison above contrasts a single attention function operating across the full model dimension against multi-head attention, which projects inputs into parallel lower-dimensional subspaces before concatenating and projecting them back to the base model dimension [p00026, p00028].

Each layer also includes a position-wise feed-forward network applied separately and identically to each position [p00035]. It consists of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation between them [p00035, p00036]:
$$\mathrm{FFN}(x) = \max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2$$
The inner dimension is $d_{ff} = 2048$, while input and output dimensions remain $d_{\text{model}} = 512$ [p00037]. Input and output embeddings share weights with the pre-softmax linear transformation, and embedding weights are scaled by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$ [p00038].

# Positional Encodings and Structural Trade-Offs Across Sequence Layers

Because the Transformer doesn't use recurrence or convolutions, it doesn't have an innate sense of sequence order [p00039]. To inject positional information, fixed sinusoidal positional encodings are added directly to the input embeddings at the base of both stacks [p00039, p00041]:
$$PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right), \quad PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)$$
The authors hypothesized that sinusoids help the model attend by relative positions because $PE_{pos+k}$ can be expressed as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$ for any offset $k$, while potentially allowing the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths unseen during training [p00042, p00043].

Evaluating sequence layers across theoretical criteria reveals self-attention's structural benefits [p00048]:
* **Self-Attention:** Operates with $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ complexity per layer, requires $O(1)$ sequential operations, and achieves an $O(1)$ maximum path length [p00048].
* **Recurrent Layers:** Incur $O(n \cdot d^2)$ complexity, require $O(n)$ sequential operations, and exhibit an $O(n)$ maximum path length [p00048].
* **Convolutional Layers:** Require $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$ complexity, $O(1)$ sequential operations, and an $O(\log_k(n))$ path length with dilated convolutions [p00048, p00050].

Self-attention's per-layer complexity is lower than recurrent layers whenever sequence length $n$ is smaller than representation dimension $d$, which is typical for subword machine translation representations [p00049].

For regularization, the base model applies residual dropout ($P_{drop} = 0.1$) to sub-layer outputs and embedding sums, along with label smoothing ($\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1$) [p00059, p00060]. Label smoothing forces the model to be more unsure, which harms perplexity but improves accuracy and BLEU [p00060]. Optimization relies on the Adam optimizer with a learning rate that warms up linearly for $4000$ steps and decays with the inverse square root of the step number [p00055, p00056].

# Empirical Translation Benchmarks and Architectural Ablations

On the WMT 2014 English-to-German (EN-DE) benchmark, the base Transformer scored 27.3 BLEU using $3.3 \cdot 10^{18}$ FLOPs [p00061]. The big Transformer achieved 28.4 BLEU with $2.3 \cdot 10^{19}$ FLOPs, surpassing the previous best ensemble (ConvS2S Ensemble at 26.36 BLEU and $7.7 \cdot 10^{19}$ FLOPs) by over 2.0 BLEU at lower training cost [p00061, p00062]. On WMT 2014 English-to-French (EN-FR), the big model reached 41.8 BLEU in Table 2 (and 41.0 BLEU in the text) after 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs, establishing a single-model state of the art at less than a quarter of the training budget of prior leading models [p00002, p00061, p00063].

Ablations on EN-DE development data confirmed the importance of key architectural components [p00066]:
* **Attention heads:** Single-head attention ($h=1$) degraded quality by 0.9 BLEU to 24.9, while too many heads ($h=32$) dropped BLEU to 25.4 [p00066, p00068].
* **Key dimensions:** Reducing key size $d_k$ to 16 or 32 hurt performance (25.1 and 25.4 BLEU), suggesting that measuring query-key compatibility isn't trivial [p00066, p00069].
* **Positional encodings:** Learned positional embeddings achieved 25.7 BLEU, performing nearly identically to sinusoidal encodings (25.8 BLEU) [p00066, p00069].

# Cross-Domain Generalization and Attention Head Specialization

To test generalization beyond translation, a 4-layer Transformer was applied to English constituency parsing [p00070, p00072]. Trained solely on Section 23 of the Wall Street Journal Penn Treebank (roughly 40K sentences), it reached 91.3 F1 without task-specific tuning, outperforming several competitive baselines [p00070, p00075]. In a semi-supervised setup with around 17 million sentences, it achieved 92.7 F1 [p00070, p00072].

Visualizing encoder self-attention at layer 5 revealed that attention heads learned distinct, specialized behaviors [p00051, p00124]. Certain heads captured long-range dependencies, such as connecting "making" to "more difficult" across intervening clauses [p00122]. Other heads exhibited behavior interpreted as anaphora resolution, where attention originating from the pronoun "its" focused sharply on its antecedent [p00123].

# Core Insights, Architectural Trade-Offs, and Unresolved Frontiers

The Transformer shows that self-attention can replace recurrence and convolutions entirely, enabling parallelized training, cutting compute costs, and improving translation quality [p00002, p00009, p00078].

Still, important limitations remain. Autoregressive decoding is still sequential, generating one token at a time [p00015, p00079]. Experiments were restricted to text, and scaling self-attention to long inputs like images, audio, or video requires local restricted attention mechanisms that weren't evaluated in this paper [p00049, p00079].

Recurrent neural networks process tokens sequentially, creating an inherent computational bottleneck that prevents parallelization across time steps. This sequential dependency severely constrains batch sizes and incurs massive computational costs when training on long sequences.

# The Sequential Bottleneck in Recurrent and Convolutional Sequence Models

Standard sequence transduction models have historically relied on recurrent neural networks (RNNs), such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and gated recurrent units, arranged in encoder-decoder structures [p00002, p00006]. These architectures compute a sequence of hidden states $h_t$ as a function of the previous hidden state $h_{t-1}$ and the input symbol at position $t$ [p00007]. This strictly sequential alignment of compute steps to token positions prevents parallel processing within training examples [p00007]. At longer sequence lengths, memory limitations restrict the batch sizes that can be trained across examples [p00007]. While factorization tricks and conditional computation improve computational efficiency, the core sequential bottleneck remains unresolved [p00007].

Convolutional alternatives, such as ByteNet and ConvS2S, compute hidden representations in parallel across positions [p00010]. However, their operational path length between distant tokens scales unfavorably [p00010]. In these models, the number of operations required to link signals from two arbitrary positions grows linearly in ConvS2S and logarithmically in ByteNet [p00010]. This makes learning dependencies between distant positions challenging [p00010]. Attention mechanisms had been used to connect representations regardless of distance, but they were almost universally coupled with recurrent networks [p00008].

# The Transformer Architecture: Global Multi-Head Attention Without Recurrence

The Transformer replaces recurrence entirely with attention mechanisms, establishing global dependencies between inputs and outputs in a constant number of operations [p00009, p00010, p00013]. The model follows an encoder-decoder structure where the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ to continuous representations $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, \dots, z_n)$ [p00015]. The decoder then auto-regressively generates output symbols $(y_1, \dots, y_m)$ one at a time, consuming previously emitted symbols as additional input [p00015].

Both the encoder and decoder are stacks of $N = 6$ identical layers [p00017, p00018]. Each encoder layer contains two sub-layers: a multi-head self-attention mechanism and a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network [p00017]. The decoder contains three sub-layers: a masked multi-head self-attention mechanism, an encoder-decoder multi-head attention mechanism, and a position-wise feed-forward network [p00018]. Every sub-layer is enclosed by a residual connection and layer normalization, producing an output of $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$ with a uniform model dimension $d_{\text{model}} = 512$ [p00017, p00018].

An attention function maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, computed as a weighted sum of the values where weights reflect query-key compatibility [p00019]. The Transformer uses Scaled Dot-Product Attention on packed matrices of queries $Q$, keys $K$, and values $V$ [p00021]:
$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$
Dot-product attention is faster and more space-efficient in practice than additive attention because it exploits optimized matrix multiplication [p00023]. However, for large key dimensions $d_k$, dot products grow large in magnitude, which the authors hypothesize pushes the softmax function into regions with vanishingly small gradients [p00024]. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ counteracts this growth [p00024]. In decoder self-attention, illegal backward connections are suppressed by masking out softmax inputs corresponding to future positions with $-\infty$ [p00018, p00034].

{Insert figure|fig1|Draw a flowchart showing Query and Key matrices entering a Matrix Multiply block, passing through Scale by 1/sqrt(d_k), an optional Mask block, a Softmax block, and multiplying with Values to yield the output.}

The schematic above illustrates the operational stages of Scaled Dot-Product Attention, which converts raw query and key matrices into attention weights through matrix multiplication, division by $\sqrt{d_k}$, an optional mask, and softmax normalization before multiplying with values [p00021, p00034].

Rather than performing a single attention function with dimension $d_{\text{model}}$, Multi-Head Attention linearly projects queries, keys, and values $h$ times with learned parameter matrices [p00026]. Scaled Dot-Product Attention runs in parallel on each projection [p00026]:
$$\mathrm{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1, \dots, \mathrm{head}_h)W^O$$
where $\mathrm{head}_i = \mathrm{Attention}(QW^Q_i, KW^K_i, VW^V_i)$ with parameter matrices $W^Q_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$, $W^K_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$, $W^V_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_v}$, and $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{\text{model}}}$ [p00028, p00029]. The base architecture uses $h = 8$ parallel heads with $d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}} / h = 64$ [p00030]. This projection allows the network to jointly attend to information across different representation subspaces without increasing total computational cost relative to a single full-dimensional head [p00026, p00030].

{Insert figure|fig2|Draw a two-panel comparison showing single-head full-dimensional attention on the left versus parallel linear projections into h heads, scaled dot-product attention per head, concatenation, and final projection on the right.}

The comparison above contrasts a single attention function operating across the entire model dimension against the multi-head design, which splits queries, keys, and values into parallel subspaces before concatenating and projecting them back to the base model dimension [p00026, p00028].

Each layer also includes a position-wise feed-forward network applied identically to each position [p00035]. It consists of two linear transformations with a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation [p00035, p00036]:
$$\mathrm{FFN}(x) = \max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2$$
The inner dimension is $d_{ff} = 2048$, while input and output dimensions remain $d_{\text{model}} = 512$ [p00037]. Input and output embeddings also share weights with the pre-softmax linear transformation, and embedding weights are scaled by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$ [p00038].

# Positional Encodings and Structural Trade-Offs Across Sequence Layers

Because the model lacks recurrence and convolutions, it has no inherent awareness of sequence order [p00039]. To inject token order, fixed sinusoidal positional encodings of dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ are added directly to the input embeddings [p00039, p00041]:
$$PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)$$
$$PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)$$
where $pos$ is position and $i$ is dimension index [p00041, p00042]. The authors hypothesized that this helps the model attend to relative positions because $PE_{pos+k}$ can be expressed as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$ for any offset $k$ [p00042].

The theoretical trade-offs across layer types explain why self-attention offers advantages for typical sequence lengths [p00048, p00049]:

| Layer Type | Complexity per Layer | Sequential Operations | Maximum Path Length |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Self-Attention | $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ |
| Recurrent | $O(n \cdot d^2)$ | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Convolutional | $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(\log_k(n))$ |
| Restricted Self-Attention | $O(r \cdot n \cdot d)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(n/r)$ |

Self-attention connects all pairs of positions in $O(1)$ sequential operations and with an $O(1)$ maximum path length, easing the learning of long-range dependencies [p00047, p00048]. Its per-layer computational complexity is lower than recurrent layers whenever sequence length $n$ is smaller than representation dimension $d$, which is standard in subword translation models [p00049].

Training regularizers include residual dropout ($P_{drop} = 0.1$) applied to sub-layer outputs and embedding sums, and label smoothing ($\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1$) [p00059, p00060]. Label smoothing forces the model to be more unsure, which harms perplexity but improves accuracy and BLEU score [p00060]. Optimization uses the Adam optimizer with a learning rate that increases linearly for $4000$ warmup steps and decays proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number thereafter [p00055, p00056].

# Empirical Translation Benchmarks and Architectural Ablations

On the WMT 2014 English-to-German (EN-DE) benchmark, the base Transformer achieved 27.3 BLEU using $3.3 \cdot 10^{18}$ floating-point operations (FLOPs) [p00061]. The big Transformer achieved 28.4 BLEU using $2.3 \cdot 10^{19}$ FLOPs, surpassing the previous best ensemble (ConvS2S Ensemble at 26.36 BLEU and $7.7 \cdot 10^{19}$ FLOPs) by more than 2.0 BLEU at lower training cost [p00061, p00062]. On WMT 2014 English-to-French (EN-FR), the big model reached 41.8 BLEU in Table 2 (and 41.0 BLEU in the body text) after 3.5 days of training on 8 P100 GPUs, establishing a new single-model state of the art at less than a quarter of the training budget of prior leading models [p00002, p00061, p00063].

Ablations on EN-DE development data validated key architectural choices [p00066]:
* **Attention heads:** Single-head attention ($h=1$) degraded performance by 0.9 BLEU to 24.9, while too many heads ($h=32$) dropped BLEU to 25.4 [p00066, p00068].
* **Key dimensions:** Reducing key size $d_k$ to 16 or 32 hurt translation quality (25.1 and 25.4 BLEU), suggesting that determining compatibility requires sufficient dimensional capacity [p00066, p00069].
* **Positional encodings:** Learned positional embeddings achieved 25.7 BLEU, virtually identical to the sinusoidal encoding's 25.8 BLEU [p00066, p00069].

# Cross-Domain Generalization and Attention Head Specialization

To evaluate cross-domain generalization, a 4-layer Transformer was applied to English constituency parsing [p00070, p00072]. When trained solely on Section 23 of the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) Penn Treebank corpus (approximately 40K sentences), it achieved 91.3 F1, outperforming several task-specific baselines despite lacking specialized tuning [p00070, p00075]. In a semi-supervised setup with roughly 17 million sentences, it attained 92.7 F1 [p00070, p00072].

Visualizing encoder self-attention at layer 5 revealed that individual attention heads learned specialized functions [p00051, p00124]. Distinct heads tracked long-range dependencies, such as linking the verb "making" to "more difficult" across intervening clauses [p00122]. Other heads exhibited behavior interpreted as anaphora resolution, where attention weights originating from the pronoun "its" focused sharply on its antecedent [p00123].

# Core Insights, Architectural Trade-Offs, and Unresolved Frontiers

The evidence establishes that self-attention alone can replace recurrent and convolutional layers in sequence transduction, yielding higher translation scores while enabling parallelized training that cuts computational costs [p00002, p00009, p00078]. 

However, important boundaries remain. Autoregressive inference remains inherently sequential, producing one token at a time during decoding [p00015, p00079]. The evaluations were limited to text, and scaling self-attention to longer inputs like images, audio, or video requires local restricted attention mechanisms that remain unevaluated in this work [p00049, p00079].

evidence.text:
**Abstract Notes**

The Abstract frames the dominant paradigm for sequence transduction—the task of mapping an input sequence to an output sequence—as relying on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks within an encoder-decoder framework, where top-performing setups use an attention mechanism to bridge encoder and decoder [p00002]. The core pain points addressed are the high training costs, limited parallelizability, and architectural complexity of existing approaches [p00002]. 

To resolve this, the authors propose the Transformer, an architecture that dispenses entirely with recurrence and convolutions, relying solely on attention mechanisms to achieve greater parallelization and reduced training times [p00002]. On the WMT 2014 English-to-German task, the Transformer achieves 28.4 BLEU, exceeding existing results including ensembles by more than 2 BLEU [p00002]. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French benchmark, it establishes a single-model state of the art of 41.8 BLEU after 3.5 days of training on eight GPUs, which is noted as a small fraction of the training cost of leading literature models [p00002]. The authors also state that the Transformer generalizes to English constituency parsing across both large and limited training data regimes [p00002]. 

Accompanying author notes detail individual design attributions: Jakob proposed replacing recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with self-attention; Ashish and Illia designed and implemented the initial models; Noam proposed scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, and parameter-free position representations; Niki evaluated numerous model variants; Llion worked on novel variants, initial code, efficient inference, and visualizations; and Lukasz and Aidan implemented the replacement codebase (tensor2tensor) [p00003]. The research was conducted at Google Brain and Google Research [p00004, p00005], and permission is granted to reproduce tables and figures for scholarly and journalistic purposes [p00001]. No figure visuals are provided in these introductory passages [p00001–p00005].

**Connection from Abstract to Section 1**

While the Abstract summarizes the Transformer's performance metrics, training efficiency, and elimination of recurrence, Section 1 contextualizes the specific architectural bottlenecks of sequence-aligned recurrent models that motivated this shift [p00002, p00006–p00007].

**Section 1: Introduction Notes**

Section 1 reviews the established dominance of RNNs, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent units, in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation [p00006]. 

The primary pain point identified in recurrent architectures is their inherently sequential computation: they generate a sequence of hidden states $h_t$ as a function of the preceding state $h_{t-1}$ and the current input at position $t$ [p00007]. This alignment of symbol positions to computational time steps precludes parallelization within training examples [p00007]. At longer sequence lengths, this limitation becomes critical because memory constraints restrict batch sizes across examples [p00007]. The authors note prior mitigation approaches, such as factorization tricks and conditional computation, which improve computational efficiency and performance; however, these methods leave the fundamental constraint of sequential computation unresolved [p00007].

The introduction highlights that attention mechanisms had already become critical components for modeling dependencies irrespective of token distance in input or output sequences, but were almost universally coupled with an underlying recurrent network [p00008]. To eliminate sequential processing bottlenecks entirely, the Transformer relies strictly on an attention mechanism to establish global dependencies between inputs and outputs [p00009]. The design rationale is to allow significantly increased parallelization during training [p00009]. In terms of training cost, the authors report that the Transformer can establish a new state of the art in translation quality after 12 hours of training on eight P100 GPUs [p00009].

**Connection from Section 1 to Section 2**

Section 1 focuses on the limitations of sequential recurrent computation and the introduction of a purely attention-driven alternative [p00007, p00009]. Section 2 contextualizes this alternative within prior non-recurrent efforts—specifically convolutional architectures and prior formulations of self-attention and memory networks—highlighting operational complexity tradeoffs across positions [p00010–p00013].

**Section 2: Background Notes**

Section 2 surveys prior methods designed to reduce sequential computation, notably convolutional neural network architectures such as Extended Neural GPU, ByteNet, and ConvS2S, which compute hidden representations in parallel across all sequence positions [p00010]. 

The gap identified in these convolutional models is that the number of operations required to link signals from two arbitrary positions increases with positional distance—growing linearly in ConvS2S and logarithmically in ByteNet [p00010]. This scaling behavior makes learning dependencies between distant positions more difficult [p00010]. 

The Transformer addresses this gap by reducing the operations required to relate two arbitrary positions to a constant number of operations [p00010]. However, an explicit limitation of this mechanism is the reduction in effective resolution caused by averaging attention-weighted positions [p00010]. The stated design rationale for Multi-Head Attention (discussed further in Section 3.2 of the paper) is specifically to counteract this loss of resolution [p00010].

Section 2 also defines self-attention (or intra-attention) as an attention mechanism that relates different positions within a single sequence to generate a representation of that same sequence, noting prior uses in reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment, and task-independent sentence representation learning [p00011]. Additionally, end-to-end memory networks are cited as using recurrent attention mechanisms rather than sequence-aligned recurrence for question answering and language modeling [p00012]. The authors conclude by identifying the Transformer as the first sequence transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to generate representations of its inputs and outputs without using sequence-aligned RNNs or convolutions [p00013].

sources.text: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

Ashish, with Illia, designed and implemented the first Transformer models and has been crucially involved in every aspect of this work. Noam proposed scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention and the parameter-free position representation and became the other person involved in nearly every detail. Niki designed, implemented, tuned and evaluated countless model variants in our original codebase and tensor2tensor. Llion also experimented with novel model variants, was responsible for our initial codebase, and efficient inference and visualizations. Lukasz and Aidan spent countless long days designing various parts of and implementing tensor2tensor, replacing our earlier codebase, greatly improving results and massively accelerating our research.

Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory [13] and gated recurrent [7] neural networks in particular, have been firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation [35]; [2]; [5]. Numerous efforts have since continued to push the boundaries of recurrent language models and encoder-decoder architectures [38]; [24]; [15].

Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states $h_t$ , as a function of the previous hidden state $h_{t-1}$ and the input for position $t$ . This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples. Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter. The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains.

Attention mechanisms have become an integral part of compelling sequence modeling and transduction models in various tasks, allowing modeling of dependencies without regard to their distance in the input or output sequences [2]; [19]. In all but a few cases [27], however, such attention mechanisms are used in conjunction with a recurrent network.

In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output. The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.

The goal of reducing sequential computation also forms the foundation of the Extended Neural GPU [16], ByteNet [18] and ConvS2S [9], all of which use convolutional neural networks as basic building block, computing hidden representations in parallel for all input and output positions. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes it more difficult to learn dependencies between distant positions [12]. In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2.

Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence. Self-attention has been used successfully in a variety of tasks including reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment and learning task-independent sentence representations [4]; [27]; [28]; [22].

End-to-end memory networks are based on a recurrent attention mechanism instead of sequence-aligned recurrence and have been shown to perform well on simple-language question answering and language modeling tasks [34].

To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence-aligned RNNs or convolution. In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention and discuss its advantages over models such as [17]; [18] and [9].

**Section 3: Model Architecture**

Prior approaches to sequence transduction predominantly rely on an encoder-decoder framework [p00015]. In this structure, the encoder converts a sequence of symbol representations $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ into continuous representations $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, \dots, z_n)$ [p00015]. The decoder then generates output symbols $(y_1, \dots, y_m)$ auto-regressively, producing one element at a time and consuming previously emitted symbols as additional input for subsequent generation steps [p00015]. ### Section 3.2: Attention

Section 3.2 establishes the general formulation of an attention function [p00019]. The mechanism is defined as mapping a query vector and a set of key-value vector pairs to an output vector [p00019]. The resulting output is computed as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight assigned to each individual value is determined by a compatibility function evaluating the query against the corresponding key [p00019]. The specific mathematical form of this compatibility function and the aggregation procedure are not detailed in this introductory section, serving instead as the foundation for the specialized implementations that follow.

### Section 3.2.1: Scaled Dot-Product Attention

Connecting to the foundational definition of attention, Section 3.2.1 specifies the authors' concrete compatibility mechanism, termed "Scaled Dot-Product Attention," depicted on the left of Figure 2 [p00020, p00025]. The inputs are defined as queries and keys of dimension $d_k$ alongside values of dimension $d_v$ [p00020]. The mechanism computes the dot products between a query and all keys, scales each product down by dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$, and applies a softmax function to produce the attention weights over the values [p00020]. In practice, queries, keys, and values are packed into matrices $Q$, $K$, and $V$ to compute the attention outputs simultaneously via matrix operations: 
$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$
[p00021, p00022].

Regarding prior approaches, the authors note that the two most common compatibility functions are additive attention and dot-product (multiplicative) attention [p00023]. Additive attention calculates compatibility using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer, whereas dot-product attention is identical to the authors' formulation except it lacks the $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ scaling factor [p00023]. Although both approaches share similar theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is faster and more space-efficient in practice because it leverages highly optimized matrix multiplication code [p00023]. 

However, prior work revealed a key limitation: while additive and unscaled dot-product attention perform similarly for small dimensions $d_k$, additive attention outperforms unscaled dot-product attention as $d_k$ becomes larger [p00024]. The authors hypothesize that for large values of $d_k$, the dot products grow substantially in magnitude, which pushes the softmax function into regions characterized by extremely small gradients [p00024]. To directly counteract this vanishing gradient effect, the explicit design rationale for Scaled Dot-Product Attention is to divide the dot products by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ [p00024].

### Section 3.2.2: Multi-Head Attention

Section 3.2.2 builds directly upon Scaled Dot-Product Attention by using it as a repeated sub-layer inside a multi-head architecture, illustrated on the right of Figure 2 [p00025, p00026]. The pain point identified with single-head attention using full $d_{\text{model}}$-dimensional keys, values, and queries is that averaging inhibits the model from jointly attending to information from different representation subspaces at different positions [p00026, p00027]. 

To overcome this, Multi-Head Attention linearly projects queries, keys, and values $h$ distinct times using learned linear parameter matrices: $W^Q_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$, $W^K_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$, and $W^V_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_v}$ [p00026, p00029]. On each of these $h$ projected versions, Scaled Dot-Product Attention is performed in parallel, producing $h$ independent $d_v$-dimensional outputs [p00026]. These head outputs are concatenated and projected by an output parameter matrix $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{\text{model}}}$, formalised as:
$$\mathrm{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1, \dots, \mathrm{head}_h)W^O$$
where $\mathrm{head}_i = \mathrm{Attention}(QW^Q_i, KW^K_i, VW^V_i)$ [p00028, p00029]. 

In their concrete experimental setting, the authors employ $h = 8$ parallel attention heads [p00030]. For each head, dimensions are reduced to $d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}} / h = 64$ [p00030]. The explicit rationale for using reduced per-head dimensions is computational: the total computational cost of the 8 parallel heads remains similar to that of running a single attention head with full dimensionality [p00030]. Visual depictions of both mechanisms are referenced as appearing in Figure 2 [p00020, p00025, p00026], but additional graphical details beyond the parallel layout and concatenation-projection flow are not provided in the text. No empirical ablations comparing alternative projection configurations or differing head counts are reported within these specific passages.

Section 3.2.3, "Applications of Attention in our Model," details the three distinct configurations of multi-head attention within the Transformer architecture [p00031]. First, in encoder-decoder attention layers, queries are drawn from the previous decoder layer, whereas memory keys and values originate from the encoder's output [p00032]. This arrangement allows each position in the decoder to attend across the entire input sequence, replicating standard attention mechanisms found in prior sequence-to-sequence models [p00032]. Second, the encoder features self-attention layers where queries, keys, and values all derive from the same source, specifically the output of the preceding encoder layer, enabling every position to attend to all positions in that previous layer [p00033]. Third, decoder self-attention layers permit each position to attend to all positions up to and including itself [p00034]. To address the constraint of preserving the auto-regressive property—preventing leftward information flow from future positions—the mechanism modifies scaled dot-product attention by masking out (setting to $-\infty$) the inputs to the softmax function that correspond to illegal connections, as referenced in Figure 2 [p00034]. The text provides no visual details for Figure 2 beyond this masking role, and no alternative masking strategies or empirical ablations are tested in this passage [p00034].

Section 3.3, "Position-wise Feed-Forward Networks," describes the sub-layer that operates in tandem with the attention sub-layers in each layer of both the encoder and the decoder [p00035]. This network is applied to each position separately and identically, comprising two linear transformations separated by a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation function, defined mathematically as $\mathrm{FFN}(x)=\max(0, xW_1 + b_1) W_2 + b_2$ [p00035, p00036]. While the parameters are identical across positions within a given layer, they differ across different layers [p00037]. An alternative framing explicitly noted is that this operation is equivalent to two convolutions with a kernel size of 1 [p00037]. Stated model dimensions specify an input and output dimensionality of $d_{\text{model}}=512$ and an inner-layer dimensionality of $d_{ff}=2048$ [p00037]. The passage does not report alternative activation functions or dimension variations.

Section 3.4, "Embeddings and Softmax," establishes the representation layers that feed into and decode from the aforementioned attention and feed-forward sub-layers. As in prior sequence transduction models, learned embeddings project input and output tokens into continuous vectors of dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ [p00038]. At the output stage, a standard learned linear transformation paired with a softmax function converts decoder outputs into predicted next-token probabilities [p00038]. To tie these components together, the architecture shares a single weight matrix among the input embedding layer, the output embedding layer, and the pre-softmax linear transformation, following prior work [p00038]. The design includes an explicit scaling step where weights in the embedding layers are multiplied by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$ [p00038]. No empirical comparisons or ablations evaluating the absence of weight sharing or alternative scaling factors are provided in this section [p00038].

These three sections link directly through the model's structural pipeline: token embeddings of size $d_{\text{model}}=512$ defined in Section 3.4 supply the initial inputs [p00037, p00038]; each block then alternately routes these representations through the self-attention and cross-attention variants detailed in Section 3.2.3 [p00031–p00034] and the position-wise feed-forward networks detailed in Section 3.3 [p00035–p00037]; finally, the decoder's representations are mapped back to token probabilities using the shared embedding weights and softmax specified in Section 3.4 [p00038].

In Section 3.5 (Positional Encoding), the authors address the limitation that the proposed architecture lacks recurrence and convolution, meaning the network possesses no inherent mechanism to make use of sequence order [p00039]. To inject relative or absolute position information, positional encodings of dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ are added directly to the input embeddings at the base of both the encoder and decoder stacks [p00039]. While prior work includes both learned and fixed positional encodings [p00039], this model implements fixed sine and cosine functions across dimensions:
$$PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})$$
$$PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}})$$
where $pos$ is the token position and $i$ is the dimension index [p00041, p00042]. The wavelengths of these sinusoids form a geometric progression spanning from $2\pi$ to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$ [p00042]. The explicit design rationale is the hypothesis that this formulation enables the model to learn to attend by relative positions easily, as $PE_{pos+k}$ can be represented as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$ for any fixed offset $k$ [p00042]. In ablation testing, the authors evaluated learned positional embeddings and observed nearly identical empirical results to the sinusoidal approach (referenced in Table 3, row E) [p00043]. The sinusoidal formulation was retained because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those observed during training [p00043]. An attached mathematical note explains that if the components of queries $q$ and keys $k$ are assumed to be independent random variables with mean $0$ and variance $1$, their dot product $q \cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i$ exhibits a mean of $0$ and a variance of $d_k$, illustrating why dot products grow large [p00044].

Section 4 (Why Self-Attention) connects directly to Section 3.5 by justifying why self-attention was selected to replace recurrent and convolutional layers despite requiring supplementary positional encodings [p00039, p00045]. The authors compare layers mapping variable-length sequences $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ to $(z_1, \dots, z_n)$ with $x_i, z_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ across three design criteria: per-layer computational complexity, parallelizability (measured by minimum sequential operations), and maximum path length between long-range dependencies [p00045, p00046, p00047]. Shorter paths facilitate the learning of long-range dependencies because forward and backward signals traverse shorter distances [p00047]. 

The structural trade-offs reported in Table 1 characterize these layers as follows [p00048]:
* Self-attention achieves a per-layer complexity of $O(n^2 \cdot d)$, $O(1)$ sequential operations, and an $O(1)$ maximum path length [p00048]. It connects all positions with constant sequential operations, whereas recurrent layers require $O(n)$ sequential operations, $O(n \cdot d^2)$ complexity, and an $O(n)$ path length [p00048, p00049]. Self-attention has lower computational complexity than recurrent layers when the sequence length $n$ is smaller than the representation dimension $d$, which the authors state is typical for word-piece and byte-pair representations in machine translation [p00049].
* Standard convolutional layers with kernel width $k < n$ exhibit $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$ complexity and $O(1)$ sequential operations, but do not connect all input and output positions in a single layer [p00048, p00050]. Connecting all pairs requires stacking $O(n/k)$ layers with contiguous kernels or $O(\log_k(n))$ layers with dilated convolutions, yielding a maximum path length of $O(\log_k(n))$ [p00048, p00050]. They are generally more computationally expensive than recurrent layers by a factor of $k$ [p00050]. While separable convolutions lower complexity to $O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$, setting $k = n$ matches the complexity of combining a self-attention layer with a point-wise feed-forward layer [p00050].
* For long sequences, the authors propose restricted self-attention, limiting attention to an input neighborhood of size $r$ centered on the output position [p00049]. This yields $O(r \cdot n \cdot d)$ complexity, $O(1)$ sequential operations, and an increased path length of $O(n/r)$ [p00048, p00049]. This alternative is not evaluated in the text and is designated for future work [p00049].
* An interpretability benefit is reported: inspecting attention distributions indicates that individual attention heads learn distinct tasks, exhibiting behavior related to syntactic and semantic structure [p00051].

Section 5 (Training) directly follows this architectural motivation by opening the description of the empirical training regime used to train the resulting self-attention models [p00052].

To this end, we add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks. The positional encodings have the same dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ as the embeddings, so that the two can be summed. There are many choices of positional encodings, learned and fixed [9].
$\begin{align*} PE_{(pos,2i)} = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}) \\ PE_{(pos,2i+1)} = cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}) \end{align*}$

where $pos$ is the position and $i$ is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from $2\pi$ to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$ . We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset $k$ , $PE_{pos+k}$ can be represented as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$ .

We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E)). We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.

To illustrate why the dot products get large, assume that the components of $q$ and $k$ are independent random variables with mean $0$ and variance $1$ . Then their dot product, $q \cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_ik_i$ , has mean $0$ and variance $d_k$ . ↩

In this section we compare various aspects of self-attention layers to the recurrent and convolutional layers commonly used for mapping one variable-length sequence of symbol representations $(x_1, ..., x_n)$ to another sequence of equal length $(z_1, ..., z_n)$ , with $x_i, z_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ , such as a hidden layer in a typical sequence transduction encoder or decoder. Motivating our use of self-attention we consider three desiderata.
One is the total computational complexity per layer. Another is the amount of computation that can be parallelized, as measured by the minimum number of sequential operations required.

The third is the path length between long-range dependencies in the network. Learning long-range dependencies is a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks. One key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network. The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies [12]. Hence we also compare the maximum path length between any two input and output positions in networks composed of the different layer types.

Maximum path lengths, per-layer complexity and minimum number of sequential operations for different layer types. $n$ is the sequence length, $d$ is the representation dimension, $k$ is the kernel size of convolutions and $r$ the size of the neighborhood in restricted self-attention. Layer Type Complexity per Layer Sequential Maximum Path Length Operations Self-Attention $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ $O(1)$ $O(1)$ Recurrent $O(n \cdot d^2)$ $O(n)$ $O(n)$ Convolutional $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$ $O(1)$ $O(log_k(n))$ Self-Attention (restricted) $O(r \cdot n \cdot d)$ $O(1)$ $O(n/r)$

As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires $O(n)$ sequential operations. In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length $n$ is smaller than the representation dimensionality $d$ , which is most often the case with sentence representations used by state-of-the-art models in machine translations, such as word-piece [38] and byte-pair [31] representations. To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size $r$ in the input sequence centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to $O(n/r)$ . We plan to investigate this approach further in future work.

A single convolutional layer with kernel width $k < n$ does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Doing so requires a stack of $O(n/k)$ convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels, or $O(log_k(n))$ in the case of dilated convolutions [18], increasing the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network. Convolutional layers are generally more expensive than recurrent layers, by a factor of $k$ . Separable convolutions [6], however, decrease the complexity considerably, to $O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$ . Even with $k=n$ , however, the complexity of a separable convolution is equal to the combination of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed-forward layer, the approach we take in our model.

As side benefit, self-attention could yield more interpretable models. We inspect attention distributions from our models and present and discuss examples in the appendix. Not only do individual attention heads clearly learn to perform different tasks, many appear to exhibit behavior related to the syntactic and semantic structure of the sentences.
