### Section 6.1: Machine Translation

* **Pain Point and Prior Limitations:** Prior state-of-the-art models for machine translation (such as ByteNet, Deep-Att + PosUnk, GNMT + RL, ConvS2S, and MoE) required substantial computational training budgets, reaching up to $1.2 \cdot 10^{21}$ floating point operations (FLOPs) for large ensembles [p00061].
* **Mechanism and Inference Setup:** Models were evaluated on the WMT 2014 English-to-German (EN-DE) and English-to-French (EN-FR) newstest2014 benchmarks [p00061, p00062, p00063]. FLOPs were estimated by multiplying training time, the number of GPUs, and an estimate of the sustained single-precision floating-point capacity of each GPU [p00065] (with capacities set to 2.8, 3.7, 6.0, and 9.5 TFLOPS for K80, K40, M40, and P100 GPUs, respectively [p00076]). Base models averaged the final 5 checkpoints saved at 10-minute intervals; big models averaged the final 20 checkpoints [p00064]. Inference utilized beam search with beam size 4, length penalty $\alpha = 0.6$, and a maximum output length of input length $+ 50$ (with early termination) [p00064].
* **Hyperparameters and Stated Rationales:** Beam search and length penalty parameters were chosen following experimentation on the development set [p00064]. The big model on EN-FR used a dropout rate $P_{drop} = 0.1$ instead of $0.3$ [p00063].
* **Reported Results:**
  * *EN-DE:* Transformer (base model) reached 27.3 BLEU with $3.3 \cdot 10^{18}$ FLOPs [p00061]. Transformer (big) achieved 28.4 BLEU with $2.3 \cdot 10^{19}$ FLOPs, outperforming the prior best reported result (ConvS2S Ensemble at 26.36 BLEU and $7.7 \cdot 10^{19}$ FLOPs; GNMT + RL Ensemble at 26.30 BLEU and $1.8 \cdot 10^{20}$ FLOPs) by over 2.0 BLEU [p00061, p00062]. Training the big model took 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs [p00062].
  * *EN-FR:* Transformer (base model) scored 38.1 BLEU [p00061]. In Table 2, Transformer (big) is listed at 41.8 BLEU with $2.3 \cdot 10^{19}$ FLOPs [p00061], whereas the accompanying text states it achieved 41.0 BLEU [p00063]. Both surpass prior single models at less than $1/4$ the training cost of the previous state-of-the-art model [p00063].
* **Limitations and Unreported Details:** The passages do not reconcile the discrepancy between the 41.8 EN-FR BLEU score recorded in Table 2 [p00061] and the 41.0 BLEU reported in the body text [p00063].

---

### Section 6.2: Model Variations

* **Pain Point and Objective:** Understanding the contribution of individual architectural choices and hyperparameters to overall translation performance [p00067].
* **Evaluation Setup:** Models were varied starting from the base Transformer ($N=6$, $d_{\text{model}}=512$, $d_{\text{ff}}=2048$, $h=8$, $d_k=64$, $d_v=64$, $P_{drop}=0.1$, $\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$, 100K steps, 65M parameters) [p00066]. Evaluation was conducted on the EN-DE development set (newstest2013) using beam search without checkpoint averaging [p00066, p00067]. Reported perplexities are per-wordpiece according to byte-pair encoding and cannot be directly compared to per-word perplexity [p00066].
* **Tested Variations and Results:**
  * *Attention Heads (Row group A):* Varying head count $h$ while adjusting $d_k$ and $d_v$ to keep computation constant showed that single-head attention ($h=1$, $d_k=d_v=512$) worsened performance by 0.9 BLEU (24.9 BLEU, 5.29 PPL) compared to the base model (25.8 BLEU, 4.92 PPL) [p00066, p00068]. Having too many heads ($h=32$, $d_k=d_v=16$) also reduced quality to 25.4 BLEU (5.01 PPL) [p00066, p00068].
  * *Key Size (Row group B):* Reducing key size $d_k$ to 16 ($d_v=64$, 58M params) or 32 (60M params) degraded BLEU to 25.1 and 25.4 [p00066, p00069].
  * *Network Depth, Width, and Capacity (Row group C):* Increasing layers ($N=8$: 25.5 BLEU, 4.88 PPL, 80M params), size ($d_{\text{model}}=1024$: 26.0 BLEU, 4.66 PPL, 168M params), or feed-forward inner dimension ($d_{\text{ff}}=4096$: 26.2 BLEU, 4.75 PPL, 90M params) improved quality over smaller counterparts [p00066].
  * *Regularization (Row group D):* Dropping dropout entirely ($P_{drop}=0.0$) hurt performance (24.6 BLEU, 5.77 PPL), while $P_{drop}=0.2$ yielded 25.5 BLEU [p00066]. Label smoothing $\epsilon_{ls}=0.0$ resulted in 25.3 BLEU (4.67 PPL) and $\epsilon_{ls}=0.2$ yielded 25.7 BLEU (5.47 PPL) [p00066].
  * *Positional Encodings (Row E):* Learned positional embeddings attained 25.7 BLEU and 4.92 PPL, nearly identical to the sinusoidal baseline (25.8 BLEU, 4.92 PPL) [p00066, p00069].
  * *Big Model:* Reached 26.4 BLEU and 4.33 PPL on the development set at 300K training steps [p00066].
* **Design Rationales and Hypotheses:**
  * The performance loss when reducing $d_k$ led authors to hypothesize that measuring compatibility is non-trivial, suggesting that compatibility functions more sophisticated than dot products might be beneficial [p00069].
  * Dropout is explicitly credited with preventing overfitting [p00069].
* **Limitations and Unevaluated Alternatives:** The hypothesis regarding alternative compatibility functions beyond dot product was not tested within the provided text [p00069].

---

### Section 6.3: English Constituency Parsing

* **Pain Point and Prior Limitations:** English constituency parsing presents unique structural constraints, generates output sequences substantially longer than inputs, and has historically seen recurrent sequence-to-sequence architectures struggle to achieve competitive results in small-data training regimes [p00071].
* **Mechanism and Experimental Setup:**
  * A 4-layer Transformer with $d_{\text{model}} = 1024$ was trained on Section 23 of the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) Penn Treebank dataset (approximately 40K training sentences; 16K vocabulary) and in a semi-supervised setting with the larger high-confidence and BerkeleyParser corpora (approximately 17M sentences; 32K vocabulary) [p00070, p00072].
  * Most hyperparameters were kept unchanged from the base EN-DE translation model; a small number of tuning experiments on Section 22 selected dropout (residual and attention), learning rates, and beam search parameters [p00073]. Inference used beam size 21, length penalty $\alpha = 0.3$, and a maximum output sequence length of input length $+ 300$ [p00073].
* **Reported Results:**
  * *WSJ only (discriminative):* The 4-layer Transformer achieved 91.3 F1, outperforming Vinyals & Kaiser (88.3), Petrov et al. BerkeleyParser (90.4), and Zhu et al. (90.4), while remaining below Dyer et al. (91.7) [p00070, p00075].
  * *Semi-supervised:* The 4-layer Transformer reached 92.7 F1, exceeding Zhu et al. (91.3), Huang & Harper (91.3), McClosky et al. (92.1), and Vinyals & Kaiser (92.1) [p00070].
  * Across all parsed baselines, the model was surpassed only by Luong et al. multi-task (93.0) and Dyer et al. generative Recurrent Neural Network Grammar (93.3) [p00070, p00074].
* **Limitations:** The parsing model relied on limited hyperparameter tuning on Section 22 rather than task-specific architectural modification [p00073, p00074].

---

### Connections Across Sections

* **Generalization from Translation to Structured Parsing:** Section 6.1 proves the efficiency and translation quality of the Transformer on large parallel benchmarks (WMT 2014) [p00061]. Section 6.2 establishes how architectural components, head counts, and regularization affect that baseline translation engine [p00066, p00067]. Section 6.3 directly leverages the baseline hyperparameter configuration developed in Sections 6.1 and 6.2, transferring it with minimal adaptation to an entirely different structured prediction task (constituency parsing) to demonstrate cross-domain generalization [p00071, p00073].
* **Inference Strategy Consistency:** Beam search and length penalty parameters ($\alpha$) configured during translation development [p00064] serve as the basis for decoding during constituency parsing, where beam size is scaled from 4 to 21 and the maximum relative output length is expanded from $+50$ to $+300$ to accommodate parse tree syntax [p00064, p00073].

### Section 7: Conclusion

#### Pain Point, Prior Approaches, and Mechanisms
Prior sequence transduction architectures predominantly relied on recurrent layers within encoder-decoder setups, or on convolutional layers [p00077, p00078]. These prior approaches suffered from training speed limitations relative to attention-only models [p00078]. To resolve this, the Transformer is introduced as the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention, replacing recurrent layers with multi-headed self-attention [p00077]. Multi-headed self-attention defines a mechanism where attention functions across representations entirely without recurrence [p00077].

#### Stated Rationales, Alternatives, and Results
The explicit rationale for moving to the Transformer architecture is computational efficiency during training alongside empirical translation performance [p00078]. In translation tasks, the model trains significantly faster than architectures reliant on recurrent or convolutional layers [p00078]. 

On empirical benchmarks, the Transformer achieves a new state of the art on both the WMT 2014 English-to-German and WMT 2014 English-to-French translation tasks [p00078]. On the WMT 2014 English-to-German task, the best reported model outperforms all previously reported ensembles [p00078]. Exact numerical scores for these tasks are not provided in this section [p00078].

#### Limitations, Future Directions, and Untested Alternatives
Current evaluated setups are limited to text, and generation remains sequential [p00079]. To address these limitations, proposed future work includes:
* Extending the Transformer to non-text input and output modalities [p00079].
* Investigating local, restricted attention mechanisms to handle large inputs and outputs efficiently, specifically images, audio, and video [p00079]. These local mechanisms are not evaluated within these passages [p00079].
* Making generation less sequential [p00079].

#### Reproducibility and Code
The code used for training and evaluating models is hosted at `https://github.com/tensorflow/tensor2tensor` [p00080].

### References Section

Passages [p00082] through [p00121] provide bibliographic references cited throughout the paper. These entries span foundational work underpinning the Transformer's subcomponents, baseline architectures, and tasks:
* **Subcomponents and Optimization:** Layer normalization [p00082], Adam optimization [p00101], dropout [p00114], residual learning [p00092], and weight tying using output embeddings [p00111].
* **Recurrent, Convolutional, and Mixture-of-Experts Baselines:** Early sequence-to-sequence and recurrent encoder-decoder models [p00086, p00091, p00116], difficulties with recurrent gradient flow [p00093], LSTMs and gated architectures [p00088, p00094, p00102], deep recurrent translation models [p00119, p00120], convolutional sequence learning [p00090, p00099], and sparsely gated mixture-of-experts layers [p00113].
* **Prior Attention Mechanisms and Memory Networks:** Attention-based neural machine translation [p00083, p00105], self-attention for sentence embedding and reading [p00085, p00103], structured attention [p00100], decomposable attention [p00108], memory networks [p00115], active memory [p00097], and abstractive summarization using deep reinforced models [p00109].
* **Subword Units, Architectures, and Syntactic Parsing:** Subword units for rare words via Byte Pair Encoding [p00112], architectural explorations in translation [p00084], Inception and Xception architectures [p00087, p00117], Penn Treebank corpora [p00106], and constituency parsing/grammar approaches [p00089, p00095, p00107, p00110, p00118, p00121].

### Section Connections

Section 7 (Conclusion) synthesizes the central claim of the paper—replacing recurrent and convolutional layers with self-attention—by linking the resulting model directly to the baseline paradigms cited in the References [p00077, p00078, p00083, p00090, p00116]. The limitations and proposed extensions in Section 7 (such as local attention for large inputs and non-text modalities) directly build upon earlier attention formulations and computer vision references cataloged in the References section [p00079, p00092, p00108, p00117]. Finally, the code release mentioned in Section 7 provides the implementation framework implementing the referenced techniques (such as Adam, layer normalization, and subword processing) [p00080, p00082, p00101, p00112].

sources.text: In this work, we presented the Transformer, the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention, replacing the recurrent layers most commonly used in encoder-decoder architectures with multi-headed self-attention.

For translation tasks, the Transformer can be trained significantly faster than architectures based on recurrent or convolutional layers. On both WMT 2014 English-to-German and WMT 2014 English-to-French translation tasks, we achieve a new state of the art. In the former task our best model outperforms even all previously reported ensembles.

We are excited about the future of attention-based models and plan to apply them to other tasks. We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video. Making generation less sequential is another research goals of ours.
